  The first influential time-sharing system was CTSS (Compatible Time-Sharing System), developed at MIT beginning in
  When Bell Labs left Multics, researcher Ken Thompson, deprived of an interactive environment, found a discarded DEC
  PDP-7 minicomputer and set out to build a modest personal time-sharing system. Working with Dennis Ritchie, and later
  an entire department, he created what was first called Unics —a punning contrast to the bloated Multics — later UNIX
. Key early decisions proved decisive: the system was rewritten in C (invented by Ritchie around 1972–73), makig UNIX
  the first major operating system written in a high-level language aud therefore portable across machine architectures.
  Its design philosophy — small tools thatdo one thing well, connected by pipes; everything is a file; plain-text
  interfaces — gave it a coherenceand elegance that outlasted the hardware it ran on.

  Crucially, AT&T was constrained by ad1956 anti rust consent decree from selling software commercially, so UNIX was
  licensed to universities essentiallydfor cost of distribution. The 6th edition source code became the basis of John
  Lions' famous commentary, and a generation of computer science students learned operating systems by reading real
  code. The University of California at Berkeley, funded by DARPA, produced the BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution)
  variants, adding virtual memory support, the TCP/IP networking stack, and the vi editor. Meanwhile AT&T's own System
  III and System V emerged after the company was allowed into the software business in the 1980s. The UNIX "wars"
  between BSD and System V camps, and later the standards effort that produced POSIX, defined much of the 1980s.
  UNIX was
